name: Makasae-Makalero
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: For words uttered in isolation and short phrases, the penultimate stress pattern is pervasive; it holds for bi-, tri- and the occasional quadrisyllabic lexical item [...] Note that lexical items in which more than one syllable precedes the stress-bearing one [...] have a secondary stress on the first syllable [...] This yields a trochaic rhythm. [...] A notable set of exceptions to this trochaic pattern is presented by words or short phrases ending in heavy syllables. [p. 90] [...] Clearly, Makalero makes use of the moraic trochee [...] The word stress thus lies on the last foot rather than on the penultimate syllable. [p. 91]
new_statements.citation: Huber, Juliette. 2011. A grammar of Makalero: A Papuan language of East Timor. PhD dissertation, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam. Utrecht: LOT (LOT dissertation series 279).
new_statements.locator: Ch. 2 Phonology, §2.6.1 Stress in isolated words, pp. 90-91 (PDF pp. 114-115)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Main stress falls on the rightmost moraic trochee, built right to left: on the penultimate syllable when the final syllable is light (fala, lolitu, isarami, and disyllabic grammatical items), but on the final syllable when it is heavy (diphthong or long vowel: kamunei, leteroo). Effectively stress on the penultimate mora. Feet are left-headed; a leftover initial light syllable is stranded.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the first syllable of quadrisyllables and of words with a heavy final ([,isa'rami], [,usu'padu], [,kamu'nei]); an initial heavy syllable forms its own foot and carries its own (secondary or near-equal) stress ([,pu:'lata] 'head', [,mi:'tini]).
new_statements.exceptions: Words/short phrases ending in heavy syllables (diphthong or long vowel) take final main stress (kamunei [,kamu'nei], leteroo [,lete'ro:], p. 90). Words with an initial heavy syllable show an extra stress on it (puulata [,pu:'lata], mit=ini [,mi:'tini], loans viitima, saapatu, p. 92-93), interpreted as compounds/multi-morphemic. Loanwords may keep donor-language stress via vowel length (viitima 'victim', p. 93).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain: isolated words and short phrases (§2.6.1); beyond the morpheme the domain of stress assignment is the phonological word, clitics like =ini and =ee can take or shift stress (§2.6.2, pp. 93-94), and stress in longer utterances is described as variable and not fully analysed. Stress is realised mainly through intensity, not length or pitch (p. 87-89). Echo vowels count as morae and shift stress (asan ['ʔasan] vs [a'sa:na], p. 92). 'I am not aware of minimal pairs with stress as the only distinctive feature.' (p. 93)
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog's language-level maka1316 'Makasae-Makalero' has two dialects: Makasai [maka1317] and Maklere (= Makalero) [makl1245]. The quoted statement (Huber 2011) describes Makalero of Iliomar subdistrict, i.e. makl1245. Makasae proper (maka1317) has the same pattern in two first-hand open sources saved alongside: Fogaça 2015, pp. 81-82: 'Em Makasae, o acento é previsível na penúltima sílaba [...] quando a última sílaba é considerada pesada, o acento recai sobre ela, sendo assim classificado como sensível à quantidade (SQ)' ('In Makasae stress is predictable on the penultimate syllable... when the final syllable is heavy, stress falls on it, so it is classified as quantity-sensitive'); and Brotherson 2003, p. 23: 'Primary stress in native Makasai words is usually placed on the penultimate syllable, with secondary stress on the preantepenultimate syllable.' So the weight-sensitive penultimate-mora reading holds for both dialects of maka1316.

sources.note: §3.7 Observações sobre o acento, pp. 81-82: 'Em Makasae, o acento é previsível na penúltima sílaba' (examples la'a, lasi, o'asi, uruwatu, utasia, utatali); but 'quando a última sílaba é considerada pesada, o acento recai sobre ela, sendo assim classificado como sensível à quantidade (SQ)' (apa 'stone' vs apaa 'mountain', asawaa 'egg', fila', ira'); §3.7.1 possible compensatory lengthening of the penult to keep it stressed (mostly Portuguese loans); p. 164 summary repeats penultimate default + quantity sensitivity. sources.note: Brief phonology sketch, p. 23: 'Primary stress in native Makasai words is usually placed on the penultimate syllable, with secondary stress on the preantepenultimate syllable.' p. 24: echo vowels after final consonants (doil > [doili], asan > [asana]) do not affect stress placement. Describes Makasai of Ossu area (maka1317).
